title: Improving the log-space SAT time exponent beyond 2 cos(π/7)
formal:
Let \(\alpha=2\cos(\pi/7)\), approximately \(1.8019377\). Does there exist a rational constant \(q>\alpha\) such that no uniform deterministic random-access algorithm decides SAT using both \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) workspace on every input of bit length \(N\)? In symbols, is
\[\exists q\in\mathbb Q,\quad q>2\cos(\pi/7)\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]?\]
This is the fixed positive improvement explicitly proposed in Problem 1. The two resource bounds must belong to the same machine.
why: A fixed improvement would cross a precisely understood limit of the established proof framework for unconditional SAT time-space lower bounds. It would strengthen our understanding of how little memory constrains computation on an NP-complete problem.
status_note: Source-open. The full 2016 column gives this concrete target. The 2007 full manuscript’s Theorem 1.2 supports the 2008 SAT threshold, the 2015 introduction/Theorem 1.1 specify the restricted proof-rule barrier, the 2021 main statements concern distinct verification classes, and the 2023 Remark 47 still records the classical simultaneous threshold. Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 found no fixed improvement matching the stated logarithmic-space SAT target. Source/model and theorem scopes were checked; no independent proof certification of the complete lower-bound literature is claimed.

progress.text: Williams’s SAT specialization obtains the threshold \(2\cos(\pi/7)\) for subpolynomial-workspace deterministic random-access computation.
Buss and Williams establish that the formalized alternation-trading rules R0–R2 cannot improve the threshold.
Problem 1 asks for a fixed positive improvement for logarithmic workspace.
A broader lower-bound framework recovers the classical SAT exponent while giving stronger bounds for different quantum and randomized verification classes.
Remark 47 still records the same simultaneous SAT threshold and distinguishes it from separate time/space alternatives.

importance.reason: A modest-looking quantitative improvement sits beyond a proved limit of a major lower-bound method. The concrete target advances the uniform SAT frontier, though one exponent alone would not settle a standard class separation.

sentences: The input is a Boolean satisfiability formula measured by its complete binary length.
The proposed lower bound applies to deterministic algorithms that use only logarithmic writable memory and can query any input location.
The goal is to exclude some time exponent strictly larger than 2 cos(π/7), with the same machine subject to both resource bounds.
Known lower bounds approach the threshold from below, and a theorem limits a formalized proof method at that threshold.
A refutation must provide algorithms for every larger exponent, possibly different algorithms for different exponents.

definitions:
SAT is satisfiability of explicitly encoded Boolean 3-CNF formulas, as permitted by the source. Each clause contains at most three literals, each a variable or its negation; the formula is a conjunction of clauses. It is satisfiable if some Boolean assignment to its occurring variables makes it true. Empty clauses are false and the conjunction of no clauses is true. The input is a fixed self-delimiting binary list of clauses, signed variable identifiers and delimiters. Identifiers can be chosen from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused names permitted. All occurrences and identifiers count in the total bit length \(N\). The encoding is explicit, and malformed strings are rejected. Size is not just the number of variables, and there is no promise of sparse occurrences or compressed access to the formula.

Fix a deterministic random-access bit-machine model: a finite Turing-machine program with a fixed number of initially blank finite-alphabet work tapes, including a tape for a binary input address. A query reads the input bit at that address in one step, returning an endmarker out of range. Constructing, changing and storing addresses uses charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only. Work heads use ordinary tape moves; every distinct work cell visited, including address bits, counters and blank cells crossed, counts toward space. There are no random bits, nondeterministic choices, advice, oracles, catalytic storage or unbounded-precision unit-cost operations. The machine halts with an accept/reject answer on every input.

For a fixed \(q\), membership in \(\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]\) means that there exist one such correct machine and constants \(C,D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with
\[\text{time on }x\le D\left\lceil(N+2)^q\right\rceil,\qquad
\text{visited work cells on }x\le C\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\]
for every binary input \(x\) of length \(N\). Bounds include parsing and malformed inputs. They are worst-case bounds with no distribution on formulas. The hidden constants may depend on the machine and on \(q\), but not on the input or its length. A different slow small-space algorithm and fast large-space algorithm do not establish this simultaneous membership.

The general-purpose random-access convention prevents a lower bound caused solely by slow movement across the input. Standard logarithmic-workspace word or work-memory random-access models can be simulated in this bit model using logarithmic space and a polynomial-logarithmic time factor. Conversely, a word machine can implement its elementary bit operations. Since the target asks for some fixed exponent strictly larger than \(\alpha\), such factors can be absorbed by choosing a slightly smaller positive improvement. This convention does not ask for a sharp model-dependent boundary at the exponent \(\alpha\) itself.

The outer quantifier chooses one \(q>\alpha\); the resulting lower bound must exclude every eligible machine and all \(C,D\). Allowing an arbitrary real exponent instead of a rational one gives the same existence question, since a rational exponent can be chosen strictly between \(\alpha\) and any proposed larger exponent. The exact trigonometric constant defines the threshold; its displayed decimal is only explanatory. A negative answer would mean that for every rational \(q>\alpha\) some eligible algorithm achieves the stated time and space bounds. These algorithms may depend on \(q\); the negation does not require a single algorithm simultaneously meeting all exponents or running in \(N^{\alpha+o(1)}\) time.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential lower-bound statement. A positive answer must specify an exponent \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\) and rule out every correct, total deterministic algorithm with simultaneous \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) visited workspace. A negative answer must establish the existence of an appropriate correct algorithm for every rational \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\), with its own fixed resource constants allowed. A result only below the threshold, for a restricted algorithm or proof paradigm, for counting satisfiable assignments, or for a larger verification class does not settle this target. Neither evidence from proof search nor an unproved hardness assumption is an unconditional solution. The exponent comparison and asymptotic quantifiers must be proved exactly; the decimal approximation and a numerical tolerance cannot replace them.

source_formulation.text: Problem 1 asks to improve SAT time lower bounds on logarithmic-space machines and explicitly proposes excluding time n raised to 2 cos(π/7) plus a fixed positive constant.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source’s concrete fixed-exponent target; rational-exponent formulation is equivalent

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space algorithm may repeatedly reread the formula while retaining very little information. Repeated reading saves memory but costs time. This card asks for a larger unconditional exponent in that time cost, with logarithmic memory kept fixed.

Williams’s lower bound rules out deterministic subpolynomial-space SAT algorithms with time exponent below \(2\cos(\pi/7)\). Subpolynomial space means \(N^{o(1)}\): smaller than every fixed positive power of \(N\), and includes logarithmic space. The target here asks to move strictly above that exponent in the particular logarithmic-space regime.

Buss and Williams prove an exact limitation of a formalized family of alternation-trading arguments. Theorem 1.1 concerns their inference rules R0–R2; these rules cannot establish a contradiction beyond the threshold. This is a theorem about those proof rules, not an upper-bound algorithm for SAT or an impossibility theorem for all mathematical lower-bound arguments.

The 2021 paper obtains stronger exponents for problems admitting quantum or randomized verification with a proposed witness. It also recovers the classical SAT threshold in its general framework. The stronger results retain their different verification classes and cannot be read as an improved SAT exponent.

The 2023 discussion separates two kinds of lower bounds. A simultaneous bound excludes a single machine that is both fast and space-efficient. A separate-algorithm alternative says that SAT cannot have both a fast algorithm and another sufficiently space-efficient algorithm. The logical forms differ, and neither removes its space qualification automatically.

Proving one larger fixed exponent would be a concrete advance, but would not by itself prove P ≠ NP or L ≠ NP. A logarithmic-space SAT algorithm, if one existed, could still have a larger fixed polynomial running time. Excluding all polynomial exponents in logarithmic space would be the stronger class separation.
